RE. LAW AND ORDER PROBLEM IN DELHI 
THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, a serious law and order situation has been created in the capital city 
of Delhi. The violent protests of workers and owners of those affected by the 
Supreme Court decision for relocation of polluting industries have left the city 
burning. Law and order in the capital city is the direct responsibility of the Central 
Government. Therefore, Sir, we demand that the hon. Home Minister should make 
a statement on this subject. 
Sir, we are all for respecting the decisions of the Supreme Court, but Sir, 
the problem that we are dealing with is a problem which has a large human 
dimension. We all want that the environment should be protected, safeguarded. 
The essential life support systems of the capital city need to be preserved and 
protected, but we cannot be oblivious to the fact that all this must be done, taking 
into account the interests of the workers and others affected by the processes of 
environment protection. We cannot preserve and protect the environment by 
perpetuating the poverty and sufferings of the downtrodden. It is in this context that 
the Government of the National Capital Territory of Delhi has been asking the 
Central Government to make suitable amendments to the Master Plan so that this 
whole problem can be looked at from a wider human angle, taking into account 
both the environmental aspect and interests of the affected workers who need 
assistance for rehabilitation, for alternat ive piece of land. We cannot take a 
mechanic view of all this. Therefore, Sir, I demand that the Government should 
make, without any loss of time, a statement on this subject. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Sir, we have been watching that 
on this issue, several Ministers have been making statements outside, in the Press, 
but it has a very complex dimension, as the Leader of the Opposition has rightly 
pointed out. This issue has been lingering on for the last five years; and, 
particularly, from this side, we have, time and again, raised our concern about the 
livelihood of the workers. Now, the total number of people affected, including 
their families, is to the tune of fifty lakhs. I think, we cannot remain a silent 
spectator to all that is happening. So, the Government should come forward to 
make a statement and take everybody into confidence

*22. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the observations 
of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India regarding the loss suffered 
by the exchequer consequent to Government's decision to allow private telecom 
operators to switch over from licence fee system to the new revenue sharing 
arrangement; and 
(b) if so, what is the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Yes, Sir. A paragraph titled "Package of concessions to existing Cellular 
and Basic Telephone Service Operators" has been included in the Report of 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the Year ended March, 1999 
(No. 6 of 2000). 
Government does not agree with the observations made by Comptroller 
and Auditor General of India. The Government considers that the policy 
regarding migration of the existing licensees to the New Telecom Policy, 1999 
(NTP-99) regime of revenue sharing arrangement was formulated as a result 
of informed and institutionalized decision in best public interest making 
pragmatic adjustments warranted by ground realities in relation to the Telecom 
Industry. The uniform application of NTP-99 which was desirable to provide 
a level playing field to all operators, was also aimed at ensuring accelerated 
growth of telecom sector by bringing in multipoly, better accessibility and 
improved / cost effective service to customers and this midcourse correction 
was considered an important instrument to achieve the objectives of the said 
policy.

 SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:

Statement

Banks' Association (IBA), Public Sector Banks and Minsitry of Finance was 
set up in June, 2000 for making recommendations on all aspects of Human 
Resource Management in the Public Sector Banks. This Committee in its 
Interim Report recommended introduction of a Voluntary Retirement Scheme 
and a Scheme for Sabbatical. IBA sought Government's no objection to

Non-Payment of Money-orders 
*35. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that non-payment of money-orders to addresses 
at distant places is a matter of the day which causes inconvenience to the 
remitter also; 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
(b) whether it is also fact that on the reporting of such cases to the 
Press these are paid on duplicate money-orders; 
(c) if so, the number of such cases detected during the last one year; 
and 
(d) the penal action taken against the guilty officers? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (d) It is not a fact that non-payment of money orders to 
addresses at distant place is a regular occurrence. Generally money orders are 
paid on time to the payee irrespective of where he is residing as per 
departmental norms for delivery. Modernization of money order service 
through the use of VSAT network is improving its efficiency. Non-payment 
of money orders cause inconvenience to the remitter as also to the payee and 
the Department is alert in dealing with such complaints, in addition to regular 
administrative steps for monitoring/transmission/payment of money orders. 
Such monitoring includes verification of paid money orders selectively by 
supervisory officials. As soon as a complaint is r eceived, it is acknowledged, 
indexed and an enquiry letter is issued to the paying office. There is a long 
standing provision in the de partmental rules that in case no reply is received 
within 10 days from the paying office, a duplicate money order is got issued 
and paid. The Department receives comp laints through various sources like 
Ministers Office, Secretary (P)'s Office, MPs/VIPs, PMO, President Secretariat 
and Directorate of Public Grievances and also directly from individual 
remitters. Complaints received through th e press are only 0.2% of the total 
complaints. Prompt and effective action is taken on all such complaints. During 
the year 1999-2000, the Department handled a total number of 11.37 crores of 
money orders and a total of 56,840 complaints about non-payment of money 
orders were received including the complaints appearing in the press. If any 
official is found responsible for deficien t service, he is suitably punished as 
per provisions of relevant rules. During the year 1999-2000, a total of 663 
officials were imposed different kinds of punishments in the country for 
complaints against postal services including those relating to money orders.

designed, tested and deployed in Telecom Network, new technology becomes 
available which enables more features  than the ones already provided. 
However, as and when such a situation arises, action is taken by C-DOT 
either to modify the design of the product or stop further development work 
in that product if it is not possible to adapt it to its new requirements. In any 
R&D activity it is but natural that all developmental projects do not 
necessarily culminate in commercially deployable product and it would not 
be correct to treat such expenditure as wasteful. 
Projects initiated by C-DOT are prop osed by the Project Board of C-
DOT in its annual business plan on the basis of user requirements and 
technology scenario globally. These are considered by the Steering Committee 
and approved by the Governing Council of C-DOT.

Expansion of mobile internet network 
141. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have a proposal to expand the mobile internet; 
(b) if so, the steps taken in that regard during the last three years; 
(c) the plan drawn up for expansion of Mobile Internet Network till the 
end of Ninth Five Year Plan; and 
(d) the details of various efforts made for the expansion of Mobile 
Internet in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) to (d) The New Telecom 
Policy-99 (NTP) envisages that Cellular Mobile Service Providers (CMSPs) 
shall be free to provide, in its service area of operation, all types of mobile 
services including voice and non-voice messages, data services and PCOs 
utilizing any type of network equipment, including circuit and/or packet 
switches, that meet the relevant International Telecommunication Union (ITU)/ 
Telecommunication Engineer Center (TEC) standard. 
As per the information gathered from Cellular Operators Association of 
India, "The Internet on Mobile Telephony has been made possible by 
introducing Wireless Application Protocol (WAP)". Some of Cellular Operators 
in India have recently started WAP se rvices and other are planning to 
progressivly introduce it. Expansion of Mobile Internet will depend on Market 
demand. There is no common plan for the whole cellular industry. Each 
operator is implementing after assessing business potential in their area of 
operation. It is very difficult to forecas t any kind of growth etc. as it is in 
infancy stage even in the rest of the world. Mobile Internet access is being 
provided by individual operators based on business potential as it involves 
additional investments. Competition rs driving the plans. 
The Ninth Five Year Plan of Department of Telecom is for expansion of 
cellular mobile and internet services and not specifically for mobile internet. 
VSNL has enabled its internet service to be usable by mobile users. 
VSNL has also provided "Webcell" Servies based on WAP. Using a WAP 
phone any mobile subscriber can acces s VSNL website, read mail and surf 
the web. 
76

As on date BSNL is yet to start Mobile Telephone Service in its Network.

adverse impact of such surge imports have been contained by a strong 
performance on the export front (by 22%) and a mild contraction in Non-POL 
imports (by 1.8%) thus resulting in a marginal improvement of trade deficit 
during April-September, 2000. 
Software service export during 1999-2000 grew by 5.3% to US $ 4015 
million on top of the increase of 49% in 1998-99. The growth rate witnessed in 
recent past is expected to be sustained during 2000-01 
The current account deficit in 1999-2000 was only 0.9% of GDP. The 
sharp rise in POL imports during 2000-01 will, other things remaining the same, 
widen the current account deficit significantly. But the buoyancy in exports of 
goods and software service exports combined with the slow growth in non-oil 
imports will help to moderate the current account deficit to a level which will be

Fall in Investment and Savings Rates 
178. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the overall investment an d savings rates of the economy 
have been falling in recent years from the peak reached in 1995-96; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what measures have been or are proposed to be taken to raise the 
saving-investment rates to a level consistent with the requirements of 7-8 
percent annual growth rate? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) The latest figures on savings 
and investment as per Central Statistical Organisation are available upto 1998-
1999. Aggregate Saving rate measured in terms of gross domestic savings as a 
proportion of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at current market prices was 
25.5 per cent in 1995-96, 23.3 per cent in 1996-97, 24.7 per cent in 1997-98 
and 22.3 per cent in 1998-99. The fall in savings rate during this period is 
114 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
attributed to a fall in the rate of public savings and rate of household physical 
savings. Similarly, aggregate investme nt rate measured in terms of gross 
domestic capital formation as a proporti on of GDP at current market prices 
was 27.2 per cent in 1995-96, 24.6 per cent in 1996-97, 26.2 per cent in 
1997-98 and 23.4 per cent in 1998-99. The fall in aggregate investment rate is 
attributed to a fall in public investment rate and also to a fall in the investment 
rate in the private sector. For increasing savings and investment rates in the 
economy it is imperative to improve the parameters which have a bearing on 
savings and investment behaviour. These include level of fiscal deficit, tax 
policies, monetary policy, inflation, efficiency of the banking system and the 
capital market and confidence in the economy. The various economic reforms 
measures undertaken so far are expected  to have a favourable impact on the 
aggregate level of domestic savings, investment and efficiency of resource 
use which is vital for putting economy on a higher growth path.

237. SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state:

going further down in PunjaL and Haryana; and

regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The 
following steps have been taken by the Government to save the subsoil water 
table in the country including Punjab and Haryana:— 
(i) Constitution of Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) under 
the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 for regulation and control 
of ground water management and development. The CGWA has

recharge projects in Punjab and Haryana have been sanctioned by

the States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate area 
specific recharge schemes to check the declining trend in ground 
water level. 
(iv) Circulation of a Model Bill to all the States/Union Territories to 
enable them to enact suitable legislation for regulation and control 
of ground water development. 
Recommendations of Water Asia Conference 
238. SHRI NANA DE SHMUKH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Water Asia 2000 Conference and Exhibition 
with latest technologies and services was held in New Delhi during September, 
2000; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that th e Conference had made fruitful and 
final recommendations for creating awareness and interest in general public 
particularly about waste water management and water conservation; and 
(c) if so, what are the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) Yes Sir. 
The Water Asia 2000 Conference and Exhibition with latest technologies and 
services was held in New Delhi between 18th September, 2000 to 20th 
September, 2000. The conference also ma de the following fruitful and final 
recommendations relating to Waste Water Management and Water 
Conservation:— 
1. There is a need for integrat ed water management through 
conservation and use of waste wate r recycling, artificial recharge 
of aquifer and rain water harvesting. Ground Water recharge, roof 
water harvesting may be incorporated in the building bye laws and 
incentive may be given to house owners to provide such facilities. 
2. In the planning of urban extensions, the availability of water, 
arrangements for collection, transportation and treatment of waste 
water and drainage needs to precede development. 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
3. There is an urgent need for adopting waste water reclamation and 
reuse practices which are technically sound, financially viable, eco-
friendly and sustainable in the lo ng run so as to reduce pollution 
load in the receiving water bodies and have water fit for use by the 
population residing in the downstream reaches. 
4. Industrial waste water in no case be allowed to discharge into water 
bodies without appropriate/adeq uate treatment conforming to 
Pollution Control Board norms. 
5. There is an urgent need to strengthen Rural as well as Urban Water 
Supply and Sanitation system by sustainable available coverage, 
quantity and quality-wise. This w ill involve people's participation 
and ensuring operation and maintenance of facilities.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Several Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes are in operation for the development of backward areas in the country in the 
form of Infrastructure Development Schemes, Subsidy Schemes and New Industrial 
Policy Package for the North Eastern Region. 
Besides, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue has declared 123 
industrially backward districts in the country for granting concessions under the 
Income Tax Act, 1961 to industrial units set up in these districts. 
176 

[21 November, 2000: RAJYA SABHA 
State-wise list of these districts classified as category 'A' & 'B' given in the 
statement (See below) 
The details of these Schemes and incentives are give below:— 
Infrastructure Development Schemes 
(i) Growth Centre Scheme: Brought into operation in 1991, it 
envisages development of 71 Growth Centres in selected backward 
areas throughout the country which would be endowed with basic 
infrastructure facilities like power, water, telecom, etc. to enable 
the States to attract industries. 68 Growth Centres have been 
sanctioned and are under development. 
(ii) Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme: Announced in 
1991 and implemented by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries 
and Agro and Rural Industries, the Scheme envisages development 
of infrastructure facilities for small industries to facilitate location 
of industries in rural/backward areas. 
Subsidy Schemes: 
(i) Transport Subsidy Scheme: Introduced in July, 1971 and recently 
extended upto 2007, this scheme is to promote industries in hilly, 
remote and inaccessible areas. Subsidy ranging from 50% to 90% 
is admissible under this Scheme on transport costs incurred on 
movement of raw materials and finished goods from the designated 
railheads/ports upto the location of the industrial units. 
(ii) Industrial Policy Package for North East: In view of its peculiar 
geographical conditions and continued backwardness, a new 
Industrial Policy and other concessions were announced for the 
North Eastern Region in December, 1997 which, besides the 
Growth Centre Scheme, HD Schemes, Transport Subsidy Scheme 
as well as Excise and Income Tax Exemptions for a period of 10 
years, has the following Subsid y Schemes exclusively for this 
region: 
(a) Central Capital Investment Subsidy Scheme: —It provides for 
subsidy @ 15% of the investment in plant and machinery subject 
to a maximum of Rs. 30 lakh to industrial units to be set up in 
identified locations. 
(b) Central Interest Subsidy Scheme: It provides for subsidy @ 3% 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
on the working capital loan to the industrial units. It was notified 
in February, 1999 and is valid upto 31.3.2007. 
(c) Central Comprehensive Insurance Scheme: It provides for 
reimbursement of insurance premium to the eligible industrial 
units. The scheme was notified on 14.7.99 and is valid upto 
13.7.2009. 
Tax Concessions: 
Under Section 80-IB of the Income Tax Act, industrial undertakings 
which begin operations after 1.10.1994 but before 31.3.2002 are entitled to a 
100% tax holiday for a period of five years in Category A industrially backward 
districts and three years tax holiday in Category B districts (refer Annexure). 
Such Industrial Undertakings in both categories of districts are entitled to a 
further deduction of 25% (30% in the case of companies) from their profits 
and gains for a period of another five years. 
Industrially backward States and Union Territories specified in Schedule 
Eight of the Income Tax Act, 1961, are also entitled to identical benefits for 
undertakings set up on or before 31.3.2002. 
(c) Does not arise. 
(d) Under die New Industrial Policy, 1991, the initiative for industrial 
development of backward areas lies primarily witii the State Governments. 
The Central Government supplements their efforts dirough various Schemes 
and incentives as detailed in reply to part (a) and (b) of the question.

18. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government proposes changes in Export Promotion Council 
membership norms; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the measures proposed to strengthen EPCs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (d) The Committee 
constituted to look into the aspects of rationalization of election procedures of 
the Export Promotion Councils (EPCs) and the criteria to be adopted for 
restructuring of the EPCs so that they retain their relevance to the national 
export effort in the context of globlisation and economic liberalization, has 
made recommendations to streamline and strengthen the functioning of the 
EPCs. The Government has since accepted the recommendations of the 
Committee and issued model guidelines to all EPCs for adoption. Guidelines 
issued concerning membership norms of EPCs and measures proposed to 
streamline/strengthen EPCs are: 
1. Membership Norms : 
With a view to giving the voting rights and right of standing for election to 
various positions in the EPCs only to such members as are having an established 
standing over a minimum period of 3 years, it has been stipulated that there will 
be two categories of members namely: Associate Members and Ordinary 
Members. A person shall be eligible for admission to the Council as Associate 
Member on receiving the Import Export Code Number from Directorate General 
of Foreign Trade in respect of the product with which the Council is concerned. 
An associate member of the Council for atleast three continuous years would be 
eligible for ordinary membership of the Council provided the company represented 
by him has to its credit during the three financial years, immediately preceding, 
average exports in respect of the product of not less than Rs. 10 lakh for SSI and 
Rs.25 lakh for other than SSI companies. The ordinary member shall have the 
right to vote at the meetings of the Council and offer himself as a candidate at 
elections to various positions in the Council. 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
2. Greater attention to importan t existing and emerging industry 
segments: 
With a view to giving greater attention to some important segments 
within an existing industry group and also to provide coverage to commodities 
or sectors presently not covered by any of the EPCs, creation of a new vehicle 
viz. Export Promotion Forum (EPF) has been proposed. Permission for creation 
of an EPF may be considered on fulfilling the prescribed conditions. However, 
such permission shall be subject to: 
(a) The members agreeing to build up a corpus of Rs. 1.00 crore when 
the society is registered which should increase to Rs.3.00 crore 
within 4 years. The principle amount of the corpus shall be 
maintained intact and the EPF shall manage its expenses from the 
interest earnings, membership fees, etc. 
(b) The members of the EPF shall continue to be members of 
concerned EPC and shall continue to pay the membership fee to 
the concerned EPC till such time as the EPF is not converted into

in a full-fledged EPC on completion of four years of its registration as an EPF.

existing EPC, there will be no minimum waiting period. On conversion into 
an EPC, it shall be eligible for MDA grants for its export promotion activities 
only. It shall also be entitled to all other benefits/facilities available to the 
existing EPCs.

contract terms as far as possible and to make the staffing structure purely 
professional over a period of five years. The existing EPCs have also been

years as applicable to the EPFs and to maintain the principal amount of the 
corpus intact and to manage its expenses from the interest earnings, 
membership fee, etc.

constituted. As and when individual service export industry builds up adequate 
demand and resources for a separate EPF, it may be allowed to break away 
from Umbrella EPF.

attention to the needs of service industries with an export potential. The Service 
Cell would also, inter-alia, advise regarding constitution of EPFs for individual 
service sectors. 
6. Election:

the vacant seats are conducted well before the expiry of the term of the retiring 
members. The elected members shall automatically retire on the completion 
of their tenures.

voting rights and the nominated/co-opted members shall not have such rights.

STATEMENT 
Salient features for establishment, maintenance and operation of Direct-to-
Home (DTH) Broadcasting service. 
(i) The applicant company shall be an Indian company, registered 
under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. 
(ii) The total Foreign Investment,* including FDI/NRI/OCB/FII in the 
DTH Broadcasting sector, shaU not be more than 49%, in which 
the share of FDI will not exceed 20%. 
Provided that the quantum represented by that proportion of the 
paid up equity share capital to the total issued equity capital of the 
Indian promoter Company held or controlled by foreign investors 
through FDI/NRI/OCB investments shall form part of the above 
said FDI limit of 20%. 
No Broadcasting Company and/ or Cable Network Company shall 
be eligible to own more than 20% of the total equity of an applicant 
Company at any time during the License period. 
Note: * Approvals for foreign equity shall be routed through the FIPB route. 
230 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Provided further that the Licensee, at all times, shall keep the 
Licensor informed of any change in the holding pattern of the 
Equity. 
(iii) The applicant company must have Indian management control with 
majority representatives on the Board, as well as me CEO of the 
Company being a resident Indian citizen. 
(iv) There will be no restriction on the number of licensees and die 
license will be issued by the Government for a period of 10 years, on 
non-exclusive basis. 
(v) The applicant company shall be required to pay an entry fee of Rs. 
10 crores, in the beginning, In addition, 10% per year of the revenue 
collected by the platform owner from channels shall be payable to 
Government as annual fee. The licensee would also be required to 
execute a Bank guarantee of Rs. 40 crores valid fox the duration of 
the licence. Licensee will additionally be required to pay the license 
fee and royalty for spectrum used, as prescribed by the Wireless 
Planning Coordination authority (WPC), under the department of 
Telecommunications. 
(vi) The Licensing Authority shall ha ve the power, after recording the 
reasons in writing, to revoke/ suspend die license in public interest. 
However before taking such action the licensing authority will give 
the licensee an opportunity of being heard. The decision of the 
licensing authority shall be final. 
(vii) For violation of license condidons, in addition to any odier acdon 
which may include revocation of license, a penalty upto Rs. SO 
crores can be imposed by die Licenser on die Licensee. However, 
before taking such action the licensing authority will give die 
licensee an opportunity of being heard. The decision of die 
licensing audiority shall be final. 
(viii) The licensee shall establish the uplink Earth Station in India widiin 12 
mondis from die date of issue of licenses. All Content provided by the 
DTH platform to die subscribers, irrespective of its source, to pass 
dirough die common encryption and conditional access system, 
located within die Eaith Station, situated on Indian soil. 
(ix) The licensee shall ensure adherence to die Programme. Code (PC) and 
Advertisement Code (AC), laid down by the Ministry of 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
Information and Broadcasting, from time to time. Record of the 
programmes and advertisements carried on the platform to be kept 
by the Licensee for a period of 90 days after broadcast and to be 
made available to the authorised representative of the Licenser, as 
and when required. 
(x) The licensee shall provide access to various contents providers/ 
channels on a non-discriminatory basis. The licensee shall not carry 
any channels prohibited by the Ministry of I&B. 
(xi) Licensee shall provide access to the Licensing Authority or its duly 
authorised representative, to all its facilities including 
equipments, records, systems, etc. 
(xii) Though licensee can use the bandwidth capacity for DTH service on 
both Indian as well as foreign satellites, proposals envisaging use of 
Indian satellites will be extended preferential treatment. 
(xiii) The licensee shall ensure s ubscriber's interests through Single 
Conditional Access Technology, Single Subscriber Management 
System (SMS), an Open Architecture (Non-proprietary) Set Top Box, 
a Cast Iron Encryption System and an efficient, responsive and 
accurate billing and collection sy stem. The Licenser shall not use 
any equipment, which is identified as unlawful. 
(xiv) The Licenser reserves the right to prohibit the transmission or 
reception of programmes in the interest of national security or in the 
event of emergency/war or similar type of situation. 
Notwithstanding any agreement between the licensee and the 
content providers, the licensee shall stop forthwith, transmission of 
TV channels or any content, as and when directed to do so by the 
Licenser or any other designated lawful authority. 
(xv) The DTH facility shall not be used for other modes of 
communication, including voice, fax, data, communication 
Internet, etc. unless specific license for these value-added services has 
been obtained from the competent authority. 
(xvi) The licensee shall obtain cl earances/approvals, as may be 
prescribed or required, from the Wireless Planning Coordination Wing 
or from the Department of Space. 
232 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(xvii) The DTH Licensee will be bound to carry channels of Prasar Bharati on 
the most favourable financial terms offered to any other channel. 
(xviii) The Licenser reserves the right to modify or incorporate new conditions 
at any time in the terms and conditions of this license, as and when 
necessary in public interest or interest of national security. 
(xix) The licensees will adhere to provisions of any legislation which may be 
brought in future with regard to broadcasting.

73.    DR. RAJA RAMANNA: 
SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: 
Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there have been many incidences of animal deaths in zoos due 
to accidents or ill treatment by the staff; 
(b) if so, what methods are proposed to stop cruelty to animals due to 
ignorance and jealousy of the staff; and 
(c) what action is being taken against those who indulged in such 
matters? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) 
This question pertains to the Ministry of Environment and Forests. However the 
information as furnished by mem is as under:— 
During recent years there has been only one case of any employee killing a 
zoo animal. On 27th July, 2000 a Caiman was found beheaded in Nandan Kanan 
Zoo. Inquiries revealed that this was done at the behest of a daily wage 
employee. The employee has been removed from service. Criminal case has 
also been launched against him. Depart mental proceedings have also been 
initiated against the staff who was on security duty in the area. A list of cases 
where animals have died due to accidents is given in the statement (See below). 
(b) (I) Keepers' Training programmes are being conducted regularly at seven 
identified centres across the country and 140 Keepers have been 
given the orientation and training during the year 1999-2000. 
(U) Regular training programmes are also organized through Wildlife 
Institute of India and IVRI for the zoo managers and the zoo 
veterinarians. 
(IH) Selected officers are also sent  for training of zoo management 
outside India. 
(c) As already mentioned in reply to para (a) the employee who was 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000]

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) to  (d) Detection of illegal and 
unauthorised constructions in die capital and action against is being taken as a 
continuous and ongoing process under the relevant provision of die Delhi 
Municipal Corporation Act, Delhi Development Act and New Delhi Municipal 
Council Act. The Ministry has also issued a comprehensive set of instructions to all 
the local bodies and agencies on 28.8.2000 for proper detection and effective 
monitoring of unauthorised constructions. These instructions include: (i) all illegal 
constructions should be demolished, not cosmetically but in toto; (ii) die cost 
of demolition should be recovered from di e illegal builders within IS days of 
demolition. In case of non-payment with in IS days, die amount due should be 
recovered as arrears of land reveune; (iii ) In all cases of illegal constructions, 
prosecution should invariably be launched against builders under die Delhi 
Municipal Corporation Act, Delhi Development Authority Act, New Delhi 
Municipal Council Act, etc. and die cases followed vigorously with the ftolice 
authorities/courts; (iv) wherever die property is on lease, action should be taken 
under the terms and conditions of lease agreement and re-entry effected within die 
shortest permissible period under such lease agreement. After re-e ntry, physical 
possession of the property should be taken by invoking die provisions of Public 
Premises Eviction Act.and damages co llected immediately. The rates of 
damages/misuse charges should be die same as per die formula followed by die 
L&DO and approved by the Ministry of Urban Development; (v) in case of DDA 
flats, where constructions have come up beyond the c ondonable limits, 
cancellation of allotment should be carried out in addition to the demolition of 
die additional construction; (vi) in cases, where after demolition, 
reconstruction is done, personal responsibility of die officer incharge should be 
fixed and departmental action 
278 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
taken against him; (vii) in cases where illegal constructions have taken place on 
rural agricultural lands, action under the provisions of the Delhi Land Reforms 
Act, 1954, should also be taken and such lands should be taken over as per 
provisions of the Delhi Land Reforms Act. Action in this respect should be taken as 
soon as the plots are cut by the colonisers and construction done in the shape of 
boundary walls, etc. In other words construction should be nipped in the bud. If it 
comes up, it should be demolished immediately. Action in this respect should also 
be taken by the concerned local agencies/DDA as per the bye-laws pertaining to 
lay out/services plans etc.; (viii) in all cases where party obtain stay/status quo 
orders, prompt action to get the stay order vacated should be taken and higher court 
moved, wherever necessary; (ix) all senior Field Officers should be asked to carry 
out physical inspection of the area under their charge and the Supervising Officer 
should also make surprise checks to ensure that the s ubordinate staff takes 
immediate action to check/ demolish unauthorised construction. Deterrent action 
should also be taken against the subordinate staff such as Building Inspectors, 
Junior Engineers, Assistant Engineers, etc. Who do not take prompt action; (x) 
Field Officers should be asked to maintain field diaries and submit them to the 
Supervisory Officer regularly. 
Instructions have also been given to the DDA and MCD to carry out 
detailed surveys to detect illegal constructions in farm houses and take effective 
action wherever such constructions are detected keeping in view the 
instructions referred to above. The matter is being monitored and followed up 
with all the concerned agencies.

ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. The World Bank have recognized 
in its reports that poverty is more than inadequate income or human development it is 
also vulnerability and a lack of voice, power and representation. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The report has made some specific suggestions to ensure 
poverty alleviation, particularly in developing countries. However, there is no simple, 
universal blue print for implementing this proposed strategy. Developing countries need 
to prepare their own mix of policies to reduce poverty, reflecting national priorities 
and local realities. Choices will depend on the economic, socio-political, structural 
and cultural context of the individual countries—indeed, individual 
communities. While the report proposes a more comprehensive approach, priorities 
will have to be set in indivisual cases based on resources and what is institutionally 
feasible. The propose strategy identifies three ways to alleviate poverty:— 
(1) By promoting opportunity through  
(i) Encouraging effective private Investment,  
(ii) Expanding into international market, 
 (iii) Building the assets of poor people,  
(iv) Addressing asset inequalities across gender, ethnic, racial and 
social divides, 
 (v) Getting infrastructure and knowledge to poor areas — rural and 
urban.

to the needs of the poor people by way of 
(i) Laying the political and legal base for inclusive development,

(iii) Promoting inclusive decentralization and community development, 
 (iv) Promoting gender equity, 
(v) Tackling social barriers,  
(vi) Supporting poor people's social capital, 
(3) By enhancing security and reducing vulnerability an encourages 
investment in human capital and in higher return activities by way of 
(i) Formulating a modular approach to helping poor people manage risk,

respond to macro shocks financial and natural,  
(iii) Designing national systems of social risk management that are 
also pro-poor,  
(iv) Addressing civil conflict,

Panic caused by the spread of brain fever (Japanese Encephalitis) In 
Epidemic form In Andhra Pradesh 
DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the Government, 
through you, to the panic caused by spread of brain fever (Japanese 
Encephalitis) in epidemic form in Andhra Pradesh. 
These days, as many as 15 districts of my home State, 
Andhra Pradesh, are reeling under the panic of brain fever or 
Japanese Encephalitis, which has taken a heavy toll of human lives in 
these districts where cases of this dreaded disease are swelling day 
after day. So far, deaths have been reported from Anantpur, Kurnool, 
Chittoor, Prakasam, Guntur, Cuddapah, Nelbre, Krishna, 
Mahbubnagar, Karimnagar and Ranga Reddy districts. But the disease 
has also spread to Hyderabad, Warangal, Nalgonda and Khammam 
districts. People are falling a prey to the disease which is turning into 
an epidemic. 
300 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
Hence, efforts are to be made on a war footing to save the 
people from this disease, particularly, the children. Hence I request 
the Central Government to send a team of medical experts to the 
affected areas of the State to augment the treatment being given to 
the patients. Adequate quantity of required medicines has to be sent 
to the State on a priroty basis. Malathion fogging has to be stepped 
up in the affected areas on a large scale. Anti-larva operations and 
insecticidal sprays have to be resorted to k ill the mosquito es as also 
the pigs and to stop their breeding. The State must be given all 
possible help to contain this disease and all precautionary steps must 
be taken against the spread of this dreaded disease. 
Thank you very much.

SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH (Manipur): Thank you, Mr.

Eastern Region. This Institute has under-graduate and post-graduate

judgment of the Supreme Court in the Bharat Coking Coal Limited

Central Government to transfer land or right, title or interests in 
relation to coal mines vested in the Coal India Limited to the 
subsidiary companies and validate certain transfers. There are eight 
subsidiary companies with the Coal India. Now they are not able to 
transfer properties which are in their names. In order to give this

property can be done only prospe ctively and not retrospectively.

India is giving power of transferring all the properties which are under 
the custody of the Coal India Limited to subsidiaries. Above all this,

SHRI NT. SHANMUGAM: Mada m Deputy Chairperson, I

Transfers and Validation) Bill, 1995 in the Hous e and also the points

Hon. Member, Shri Bhatt, talked about the challenges of coal 
import and rationalisation of railway freight. Hon. Member, Shri 
Agarwal, spoke on the collection of stamp duty, the corruption in Coal 
India and the need for reorganisation of Coal India. Hon. Member, Shri 
Thirunavukkarasu, explained the provisions of the Bill and welcomed 
the Bill. Hon. Member, Shri Jibon Roy, felt that the Bill is legally not 
correct. 
He also mentioned that the present strike in Coal India Ltd. is 
due to this Bill. Hon. Member, Shri Margabandu, felt that the Bill would 
lead to privatisation. Shri Eduardo Faleiro talked about the coal mafia 
and issues relating to tribal land. Hon. Member, Shri S.S. Ahluwalia, 
talked about the history that led to the introduction of this Bill. He has 
also mentioned in detail about the latest coal-mimrtg technology, the 
linkage of coal with power production and issues realtihg to 
subsidiaries like ECL, BCCL, etc., and mine safety. Mine safety is 
governed by the Director-General of Mine Safety. There shall be no 
change in that position.  He has also mentioned

RAJYA   SABHA       [21 November, 2000] 
that mine safety should be taken up on a priority basis and that 
categorisation was not done properly. Hon. Member, Shri Gupta, said, 
"coal is black gold". He has also mentioned that the mines are not 
modernised and mine safety is ignored. He has mentioned about the 
underground fire also. He wanted a National Coal Policy to be 
formulated. 
The Bill has a restri cted purpose of  empowering the Central 
Government to direct the transfer of the land and its rights pertaining 
to all coal-mines or coke-oven plants vested in the Coal India Limited 
or.In a subsidiary company to any or other subsidiary company of 
Coal India Limited. This Bill is not in any way related to railway freight 
re-organisation of Coal India Ltd., import of coal, de-notification of 
tribal lands and transfer of land to multinationals, etc., nor is it a proxy 
for privatisation of coalmines. 
Now, I may point out that the absence of a formal legal title to 
the land, coke-oven plants, mining rights and other properties in the 
subsidiary companies of Coal India Limited has exposed them to 
litigation and other legal infirmities. This matte r was examined by the 
Committee on Public Undertakings. The Committee had directed that 
the transfer of rights in and over land and properties in favour of 
subsidiary companies, which are de facto managing the mines and 
properties vested in Coal India Limited, should be effected without any 
further delay. Two former Attorney Generals had also advised that this 
situation needs to be rectified through appropriate legislative 
measures. The Standing Committee on Industry also undertook a 
comprehensive examination of many of the issues raised during the 
discussion. The Report of the Standing Committee, which was laid on 
the Table of the Rajya Sabha on 27.7.2000, deals with these issues at 
length and, therefore, it may not be necessary for me to go into them 
again. The Committee had recommended adoption of this Bill. 
It has been pointed out that the same objective could have 
been achieved by effecting suitable amendments in the Coal Mines 
Nationalisation Act, 1973, instead of introducing this fresh Bill. It needs 
to be appreciated that lands, mining rights and other properties have 
been acquired by Coal India Limited through various Acts, that is, the 
Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, the Coal Mines 
Nationalisation Act, 1973, the Coal Bearing Areas (.Acquisition and 
Development) Act, 1957 and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and 
through direct negotiations. An amendment to the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act would not have covered the lands and properties 
acquired through other statutes and modes. Hence, there is the need 
for a separate Bill.

Notifications of the Ministry of Finance 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): Sir, I lay on the Table: 
I. A copy each (in English and Hindi) of the following 
Notifications of the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue), 
under sub-section (1) of section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962, together 
with explanatory memoranda on the Notifications:- 
1. No.  142/2000-Customs, dated the 21 s1 November, 
2000 seeking to amend Notification No.16/2000-
Customs so as to revise the concessional rate of 
basic duty of Customs applicable to edible oils (both 
crude and refined). 
2. No.  144/2000-Customs, dated the 21 s' November, 
2000seeking to amend Notification No. 61/2000-
Customs, dated the 12th May, 2000 so as to exempt 
specified edible oils from the levy of surcharge. 
II. A copy (in English and Hindi) of the Ministry of Finance 
(Department of Revenue) Notification No. 143/2000-Customs, dated 
the 21st November, 2000, seeking to amend Notification No.18/2000-
Customs, dated the 1st March, 2000 so as to prescribe Nil rate of 
Special Additional Duty on specified crude vegetable oil of edible 
grade., under sub-section (1) of section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 
1975, together with an explanatory memorandum thereon.
